MR. ROSE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUMMER 73 YOUTH EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the announcement made yesterday by the Secretary of State having to do with an $85.4 million youth package called Summer 73.
I feel that my privileges as an elected member of the House have been infringed because the announcement of this new program, involving a huge expenditure, was not made in the House. It was made to the press outside the House before any member possessed any information at all as to the scope and thrust of the program. This somewhat unparliamentary procedure on the part of the Secretary of State interfered with the privileges of hon. members inasmuch as by his action he effectively denied those who are interested in following the program the opportunity to make observations and comments in the House.
I call upon the Secretary of State to desist from this practice of issuing press releases on such occasions and to correct his initial insensitivity to the rights of parliament by making a statement on motions today, fully explaining to the House the nature of the program, Summer 73.

subtopic: MR. ROSE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUMMER 73 YOUTH EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MR. ROSE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUMMER 73 YOUTH EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext: A shocking affront to parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subtopic: MR. ROSE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUMMER 73 YOUTH EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that the member for Trinity smiled when he made that remark. Perhaps I might comment briefly on what was said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West. It seems Your Honour is not likely to rule that there is a question of privilege here, but there may be a question of propriety which I should like to clarify. I considered very carefully whether or not I should announce this program in a statement on motions. I would remind hon. members that this is the third year in which this program has been pursued and that no substantial changes have been made. Essentially, it is the same mix as in previous years. In these circumstances, I proceeded by way of an announcement.
The hon. member says he was not given notice. I went out of my way to provide him with notice two and a half hours before meeting with the press. At about 12.30 p.m. the documents were in his office, and at roughly the same time they were in the offices of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and of the spokesman for the Social Credit party in order that the spokesmen for all the political parties might have a chance to comment. There was no attempt made to affront parliament The rationale was that this was the third year in which this program has
been introduced and I felt that a statement on motions was not justified.

subtopic: MR. ROSE-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUMMER 73 YOUTH EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM OUTSIDE HOUSE
speechtext: And the third year the announcement was made outside the House.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the other day in response to questions by the hon. member for Provencher and the hon. member for Meadow Lake I gave information which I now know, to my regret, was incorrect. I would like to remedy that error. It was in connection with the eligibility of local improvement districts for local initiative project grants. I am now informed that in both of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba by agreement between the federal government and the provincial governments local improvement districts are in fact eligible for local initiative project grants. I regret any inconvenience that this misinformation might have caused.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, January 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. J. Blais for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me congratulate you on your nomination to this high and distinguished post of our parliamentary system. The mover (Mr. Blais) and seconder (Mr. Blaker) of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne have no doubt recognized the wisdom and impartiality of your decisions for the last two sessions in proposing that you be entrusted with the chair again.

I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) on his nomination as Deputy Speaker and compliment the hon. members for Beauhar-nois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) and Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) on their reappointments.

I should be remiss, Mr. Speaker, should I fail to commend the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I should also like to congratulate the new members of the cabinet and as agriculture in my constituency is very important I am very pleased with the nomination of the hon. member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Whelan) as Minister of Agriculture. I am convinced that he will discharge his duties so well that he will gain the respect and confidence of all Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to represent a constituency that was once represented by one of our greatest prime ministers, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King.
I should like to take this opportunity to express once more to my fellow citizens of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell how grateful I am for the trust they put in me.
As I said, my riding is almost entirely rural, made up of family farms, several of which cover only 100 to 150 acres.
It is common knowledge that farmers find it difficult to survive. Whether they are in the dairy, agricultural or cattle-raising fields, their problem remains the same. We strongly believe that the prices they have to pay for feed grain are much too high.
I have even been told that the prices of concentrates for balanced feed have increased to the point where our farmers have to cut down on concentrates in those to the detriment of the quality of their cattle.
We believe that brokerage firms are taking advantage of our farmers whenever there is a strong demand for those products, particularly the concentrates.

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. Ethier
I was pleased to hear in the Speech from the Throne that the government will be taking appropriate steps concerning feed grain which, I hope, will bring about better price control.
Concerning crop insurance, I also note that the government will assist provinces, which will allow farmers to benefit from a reduction in premiums.
I also appreciate that action will be taken to stimulate tourism in Canada. As my riding is situated between the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers and bordered by Quebec and the federal capital, space can readily be created there for development of tourist centres, in co-operation with the provincial government.
Mr. Speaker, with the present minimum wage it is almost impossible to bring welfare recipients back to work. In many cases they receive over and above what labour receives for a 40-hour week at the minimum wage. May I suggest as an incentive that the minimum wage be raised to $2.25 an hour.

Old age security pension plan improvements were announced and I hope that this will include a lowering of the retirement age to 60, especially for those who benefit from the guaranteed income supplement.

Since concern for the tourist industry was manifested in the throne speech, we would appreciate very much a helping hand for the organizers of the worldwide Glengarry highland games, for grants such as for the construction of additional seating capacity to accommodate the ever-increasing number of visitors at this annual event which takes place in Maxville, Ontario, either at the end of July or early in August and at which hundreds of pipe bands and athletes of Scottish culture from all over the world meet in competition. Record crowds of well over 25,000 witness this colourful event every year. May I take this opportunity to invite all of you to visit us at this great festival.

In short, I am amazed at the contents of the Speech from the Throne and I believe that all the other members of the House feel the same. Undoubtedly, some took the liberty of criticizing it, but I suggest that this is only from habit without even evaluating its contents and its beneficial effects for all Canadians.
I was under the impression that the duty of Her Majesty's loyal opposition was to criticize constructively, but I can only express my disappointment at seeing many members on the front benches notably the member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), who dared speak without the approval of the Speaker, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) who continuously interrupts members speaking to the House, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), with all his parliamentary practice and former Prime Minister, who likes to waste the time of the House by speaking of phrenology, and of how he is proud and happy to have amongs them a 20-year-old member.

Mr. Speaker, the behaviour of the official opposition's veterans sets a very bad example for these young members of the House. I am persuaded that if Her Majesty had witnessed the behaviour of her loyal opposition, she would have asked that the word loyal be omitted.

After having witnessed all the unparliamentary behaviour on the part of the official opposition front benches I was greatly surprised to hear a radio commentator say that the Conservatives were really effective at the beginning of this twenty-ninth parliament. Either this commentator was not serious or there are two meanings to the word "effective", or else this is just a cover-up for their real ineffectiveness. On the same station I even heard the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) using strong language and demanding that the government introduce legislation before taking the customary time to debate the throne speech. Is the hon. member suggesting that we do away with traditions? [Translation]
On Sunday January 14,1 heard the leader of the Quebec wing of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), repeat that Quebec more than any other province needed help from the federal government. During his election campaign, why then did he not object when candidates of his party made political hay outside Quebec saying that province had been privileged by the former minister of DREE (Mr. Marchand)? Why did the hon. member not reply to the question he was so eager to answer during the election campaign, namely what would his attitude be were Quebec to be given a separatist government? On television he replied that the question was hypothetical, but during the election campaign he did say that if Quebec demanded separatism, as a Quebecer, he would submit to whe will of the people. There is an example of irresponsible politics, for the guidance of the hon. member who claims to be a federalist, for a single amendment to the constitution would allow a province to separate. I ask the hon. members of the NDP and the Social Credit to beware of such irresponsible people.
I wish to congratulate the hon. leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for having acquired the young MPs I have had the pleasure of meeting. To my mind, they are true gentlemen. Might I suggest that he make room, in front, for those gentlemen and room, at the back, for irresponsible members?
Mr. Speaker, I close by saying that I am proud of all the people in my riding especially because, back home, unity truly exists.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my speech I should like to congratulate you on having been elected to the high office which you hold. Having questioned your fairness in the past may I say now that at all times you were fair, that you honour your position, and that you lend great dignity and fairness to your rulings in the House of Commons.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
January 16, 1973

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would also like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). His respect for parliamentary debate and for this chamber will stand him in good stead in the difficult months ahead when he will have to preside over the House from time to time.
I would also like to congratulate the mover and the seconder, the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) and the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker). It is an honour to them and to their constituents that they should be given this task and they did an admirable job.
Having said all that, may I say at the outset that the kind of speech I will make is one I really do not wish to make. It is one that brings me no real pleasure and, in fact, a certain amount of sadness because in my speech I will deal with western Canada. Why should I deal with western Canada? The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a number of references to western Canada in the Speech from the Throne. He spoke about having a conference with the four provincial governments, and he spoke about some kind of industrial growth that should and may take place in western Canada in the years ahead. He wondered in the Speech from the Throne why the Liberals lost the west. I will try to explain why they lost the west and how they could perhaps capture it if they rethought their whole policy.
During the campaign I said that with three major changes in the Liberal party program and policies they could succeed. None of them had anything to do with the Official Languages Act or the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is from Quebec. The surprising thing about the cabinet reshuffle, the Speech from the Throne, and remarks made by ministers in this debate is that they do not show any change of heart. The Liberals have really not learned anything about western Canada.
Shortly after the cabinet reshuffle there was an article in Time magazine on the Prime Minister, in which he was reported as saying that the government's policies were good but the salesmen were poor. Now they are bringing in better salesmen to sell the policies that they believe are good. Mr. Speaker, the west did not object to the salesmen. although indeed the Liberals did have poor salesmen. The policies were wrong.
The Prime Minister visited western Canada in 1970 and talked about a particular farm bill, one that he still seems to have on his mind. He said it was a good bill but "the problem out here is that you have been listening to false prophets." I did not like being called a false prophet and so I remember that remark.
Many times Canada is likened to a marriage between the French and the English, between Ontario and Quebec. Western Canada came along after 1867, and we are not the children of that marriage. We do not want to be treated like children, to be seen and not heard. We want to take our rightful place and have some say on the direction in which this country goes and should go. We believe that ours is the most vigorous growth area in Canada. We demand our right to have a say on the direction in which we should go. The change in salesmen will not help the Liberal party one bit.
The Address-Mr. J. H. Homer

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Liberals must rethink their basic concepts of western Canada. They must rethink their policies, and they must do this before the provincial conference mentioned in the throne speech takes place.
Speaking about co-operation the Prime Minister once said, with reference to the government, that it should meet the obligation to consult and not merely to inform. I hope he remembers that when he goes to western Canada to attend that conference. But by his cabinet shuffle he has not demonstrated that he is learning or rethinking any of the three policies I will mention in a moment.
What are the three policies that ruined the Liberal party and caused them to lose the west? Mr. Speaker, western Canada is not too far away from the pioneer spirit. Many familes and young people in western Canada still have a great deal of admiration for their forefathers who came out west and fought nature and the other hazards of life. They are proud of their forefathers' fight to own their own land. What did the Liberal party do to cause them to lose votes all across the west? They brought in a capital gains tax which makes it pretty difficult for a farmer to hand down his land to the next generation.
The average farmer is proud of his father's work in harnessing nature for his benefit. He wants to pass on his land to the next generation. All kinds of warnings were given about the capital gains tax. It was pointed out that it would affect the cost of farm machinery, the transfer of land and the basic herd. But the government plowed ahead with that legislation. In fact it introduced closure. That legislation has hurt western Canada, a region which has a lot of land and few people, but those people are proud of their land. That was a mistake and it cost the Liberals thousands of votes all across the Prairies. Unless they rethink that concept they will be in for more difficult times in western Canada.
In case hon. members ask why I say this I suggest that they read the CCH Report entitled "Farmers and the White Paper on Tax Reform," in the foreword where it states:
Perhaps the single taxpayer group most dramatically affected by the government's white paper on taxation are the farmers of Canada. Whether by design-or through inadvertence-the farming community as it exists today faces virtual extinction-
Those are pretty strong words.
In the October, 1972, issue of Country Guide the president of the Agricultural Economics Research Council of Canada issued this warning about the tax changes:
Failure to become familiar with tax management generally, and to do some important things now, could result in a farmer's family farm being killed within ten years.
Those are not the words of idle politicians. They are the words of factual men who know what they are talking about. All this has caused great panic in western Canada.
The blame rests on the government, on the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet from western Canada who did a poor job of convincing the Prime Minister that the capital gains tax was wrong. I may say that the electors did a lot better job on October 30.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. J. H. Homer

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The other basic thing people must understand about western Canadians is that those engaged in the agricultural industry love to produce. But before dealing with that I wish to mention one other thing not connected with the famous Bill C-176. One other concept that the Liberals failed to understand was that their tax reform legislation was hard on the oil and gas industries, on the resource industries in general. Mr. Mahoney, the former member for Calgary South, insulted the very people who sent him here. It is no wonder he did not come back. Any member of this House who forgets the people who sent him here should not come back. His was one seat that I could bet would be lost by the Liberals.
Another seat lost through Liberal ignorance was that of the former member for Medicine Hat and former minister of agriculture, a friend of mine who has a ranch in my constituency. Where did he make his mistakes? At the wish of the Prime Minister he attempted to pilot the famous Bill C-176 through the House. At that time, Mr. Speaker, I was accused of being a terrible person, a false prophet and everything else.
Was it I alone who blocked the passage of that bill? Recently the Prime Minister admitted on a radio show that even having got it through the House the Liberals suffered a defeat. They did not get what they wanted. They did not get the rigidity and the controls they wanted. As I say, western Canadians love to produce. They know they can produce. They want the opportunity to produce. It is born and bred in them. Hon. members opposite must understand that.
Westerners saw in Bill C-176 an attempt by somebody to harness their production, to regulate and control it, and perhaps even to hinder the free flow of their goods into the thickly populated area of eastern Canada in order to serve the 12 million people in Ontario and Quebec who should be able to enjoy their produce. Bill C-176 was wrong.
Was it a political move on my part? Some people have accused me of opposing the bill for political gain. Was it Jack Horner alone who opposed it? Mr. Runciman, who has accepted appointments from the government to serve on a number of committees, had great fears about that bill. He said so in his brief to the agricultural committee. The Liberals should have harkened. The late William Parker, a strong westerner, a strong Liberal, a former president of the Manitoba Pool, said the bill was wrong and, if passed as proposed, western Canada would be hamstrung.
The Liberals should have harkened to men like that. Debate on the bill dragged on for a year and a half. Some 50,000 coupons, the greatest coupon mailing ever, more than those received in connection with the white paper on taxation, landed in Ottawa from the three prairie provinces. The people there must have been stirred up about the bill. The Liberals should have dropped that bill in order to set aside the fears of western Canada. The late premier of Saskatchewan and his minister of agriculture, both Liberals, expressed fears about what the bill would do but the Liberals plowed on with it. The Prime Minister said it was a good bill and that the children out there had been listening to false prophets. That is what he said and

we did not like it, Mr. Speaker. We demonstrated that on October 30.
What about the former minister of agriculture? Can you imagine the possibility of his winning after having been elected at one time as a Social Crediter, that group which is supposed to be to the right in our political structure? In Winnipeg on March 13, 1972, he made a speech which was reported in the Regina Leader-Post under the heading "Market Structure Said Need". In the article the former minister is reported to have said:
Free trade is a great thing when it works, but unfortunately there aren't enough constraints within the free trade system for us to accept that this is the way marketing will be.
The article then mentioned the minister's recommendations and suggestions. That smacks of socialism to western Canadians. In Alberta we live next door to Saskatchewan and so we know what socialism has done there. We want no part of it, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: How could a former Social Crediter make such a suggestion? Had his basic philosophy changed? No, Mr. Speaker, he was a servant of those above him in the Liberal party-the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt, our intellectual socialists.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: With a lust for power.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Olson was merely their servant and the people of Medicine Hat knew that and did not like it. They wanted him to serve them, not his masters in the Liberal party, so they rejected him on October 30. There were editorials like the one which appeared in the Free Press Weekly of April 17, 1971 headed "Cattle Double-crossed". There is still a bit of the old pioneer spirit left in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. A handshake is a handshake and a man's word is good. The people do not like someone who is suspected of double-crossing them so the former minister of agriculture was rejected.
I am sure there are many Liberals who have been tearing out their hair, wondering why the sales of wheat did not help them. In the 15 years I have been in Ottawa I have heard many easterners say that the man who sells the wheat reaps the political benefit, that all you have to do in western Canada is sell wheat. But why did the Liberals not reap the benefit? Why is it that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt came back from Saskatchewan alone, the only Liberal member representing the farmers there? One reason he came back was the $90,000 he spent; that sometimes helps. Part of his riding includes the city so perhaps those people were not aware of what was going on. What was wrong, Mr. Speaker? Surely this government want to know and is interested in changing its ways.
Two weeks before the election the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt announced an increase of 30 cents a bushel in the initial price for wheat. The farmers were insulted, Mr. Speaker; that was their own money and they were going to get it anyway in the final payment. They said, "Does he think we are so stupid that he can bribe us
January 16, 1973

with our own money?" If the minister knew that the international price was about to increase-he should have known it three months before October 15 when he made that announcement-he should have had the courage and the confidence in the cabinet to take a stand and increase the initial price of wheat at that time. He lacked something; he certainly lacked any understanding of the farmers when he insulted them with an increase of 30 cents of their own money. Politically he would have been farther ahead to make the announcement after the election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He was just imitating the Prime Minister.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, he is an intellectual socialist just like the Prime Minister. In my definition a socialist believes that someone has to make decisions for the masses and the masses will follow. An intellectual socialist believes he is so far above the masses that he can make the decisions and the masses will follow. But sometimes one who considers himself so far above the ordinary people forgets, and that is exactly what happened with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt and the Prime Minister in the last election.
What other mistakes did they make, Mr. Speaker? Yesterday the minister said that the Lift program had created freedom in agricultural marketing and that everything was now moving well because of it. In case anybody has forgotten what Lift is, it means "Lower Inventory For Tomorrow". When the election came along the price of grain was going up. At that time it was about $2.60 a bushel but the farmers did not have any wheat. Many of them had already delivered. During the campaign I drove to the elevators and the farmers told me that they had delivered the six-bushel quota and had nothing left to deliver except their seed for spring planting though they would have liked to be in a position to deliver wheat.
What did the Lift program cost the farmers? As the minister admitted yesterday, because of the restrictions placed upon them they grew 200 million bushels less wheat than previously. The price of wheat today is a little over $3 a bushel so any grade three student can calculate the loss to western Canada: it is $600 million through operation Lift.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Could the minister say that he did not know about the crop failures in Russia and China, that he thought Lift was a good program and now knows that he was wrong and ask for forgiveness? No, Mr. Speaker, he still says it was a good program. How can farmers be convinced of that when they have lost money on it? They are not so stupid, as the intellectual socialists found out on October 30.
What else did the minister do that was wrong? He attempted to bring in a grains stabilization bill. That was a failure and never got through the House. The whole concept was wrong; it began by trying to empty the elevators and to curb western Canada's desire to produce. The farmers did not like that at all. Operation Lift was a perfect example and they rejected it.
What does the Canadian Wheat Board have to say today? I have here a letter I received recently from the
The Address-Mr. J. H. Homer
Canadian Wheat Board which was addressed to all grain producers. The letter inquires how much grain I will have for sale in the coming crop year and states:
-every additional bushel of grain that can be made available will be needed.
The letter goes on to say that they do not have much confidence in the figures provided by Statistics Canada so they are approaching producers directly. I have been farming for 25 years but I never received a letter like this from the Canadian Wheat Board before. The letter states further:
-we need a reliable figure before we can determine how much grain we can commit for forward sales to take advantage of the higher price levels.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, they are turning down sales today because they do not know how much grain they will have. That is an alarming letter, Mr. Speaker, and points out the fact that the concept of cutting off production in western Canada was wrong. We do not want the minister to go out to western Canada saying it was right. It was wrong and we will continue to reject it.
In a news release which I issued in December I said that the fixed price of $1.95) should be the floor price and it should move upwards with the international price. I told the farmers that they were losing $30 million a year. The minister must have thought my statement was effective because the next day he issued a press release. It pointed out that the minister said the government is paying $57.5 million to assure that the farmer will receive $3 a bushel for his wheat. This was paid under an acreage payment.
There was a great deal of fanfare last January because the minister had finally made a tremendous breakthrough. This was suggested in an editorial in a western paper. The minister had now firmly established a two-price system for wheat and the farmers would get a fair return. What did this turn out to be? It turned out to be nothing more then an acreage payment. The minister fooled the weekly papers.
An editorial in the Western Producer headlined "Not Exactly A Reality" states:
It appears we were somewhat hasty when we wrote the headline "Two-price system for wheat a reality" ... in our February 3 issue.
What Mr. Lang did not say was that in an election year, there's a tendency to avoid any distribution of funds that takes in only part of a group, and that, we believe, would be the prime consideration when the decision was being made.
The minister fooled the wheat farmers. He did not help them at all. Another editorial was headlined "Two-price Or Two-face?". I said a while ago that in western Canada people still honour a man's word and a handshake. They cannot yet accept a doublecross or "two-price or two-face". We may be able to accept this some day, but not yet. I quote from this editorial:
The Minister responsible for the Wheat Board happily proclaimed that the government "has finally faced up to an issue which confronted successive governments for 20 years." ... This most recent announcement, however, shows that we are still following a policy of "Do nothing until you have to, then do anything to keep them quiet".

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. Whelan
Is that not the way you treat children? We in western Canada no longer want to be treated as children.
The Speech from the Throne refers to two other matters which are going to be dealt with, crop insurance and an equitable price for feed grain. I wish to issue a word of caution and warning. I have thoroughly studied the Canada Grains Council report on the pricing of feed grain and what they refer to as the fair formula. This is not a saleable product in western Canada. If anyone wonders why it is not, I suggest he read page 9, chapter 3. It clearly explains how the fair formula will work. It sets up a great bureaucracy which the average farmer will not take time to understand or figure out. He will feel that the price of his grain is being subsidized and that it is not going to work to his advantage.
I also wish to refer to development at Vancouver. It is a well known fact that when the minister in charge of the Wheat Board was in Calgary he said that the government was going to spend money in Vancouver. He did not say how much or how they were going to do this.
I have an article which states that Mr. Hope of the Canadian Wheat Board suggests that something must be done in Vancouver as more storage is required. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board does not realize that in the past years the expenditures in Vancouver have been curtailed, not enlarged. The government must come up with a policy for the development of a port at Vancouver which will allow our grain to move freely through that port. There are continuing reports in western papers calling for improved facilities at the port of Vancouver. The Canadian Wheat Board is having difficulty moving grain through that port because of strikes, including one that is still not settled. This is certainly a disturbing factor in western Canada.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I regret that after being here 15 years I must make a speech dealing with one region of our country. I have outlined three basic policies which went wrong and I hope the government will correct its ways. Maybe people in western Canada will then vote Liberal again. If the government does not learn to understand this better than they have in the past four years and continues to treat us as children, we will continue to reject their party, no matter from what area the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) may come or what official language he may use. It will not really matter. We will continue to reject anyone who treats us as children. We want to be equal partners and play a part in this great country of ours.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I first want to take this opportunity to congratulate Your Honour on being re-elected Speaker of the House, not only because of your knowledge of House procedure but also because I have learned since accepting this office of your knowledge of agricultural problems in the constituency you represent.
I also want to take this opportunity to congratulate the Deputy Speaker. I have known him as a man's man in this House. I know he will do a good job. I have also known for quite some time the other officials who have been elected and the same goes for them.

I wish to thank hon. members for the good wishes they have sent me on my appointment to the portfolio of Minister of Agriculture for Canada. In those thanks I wish to include the members of the opposition. Some, even Members of Parliament, may be amazed at the number of letters, calls, visits, etc. that I received from many members of the opposition. I believe they were most sincere in their congratulations and offers of help to make this portfolio and department a successful venture. I also wish to thank the members on the government side for their good wishes, of which there were many.
I received letters from people I have known in agriculture and parliamentary organizations all over the world. I was utterly amazed to know that people all over the world watch to see who is going to be responsible for agriculture in Canada. Too often we take it for granted that agriculture is not all that important, but this has brought it closer to home for me and made me realize in a different way how much importance people in other parts of the world place on agriculture in Canada because of the great industry it is and the leadership it provides for agriculture in other parts of the world.
More especially, I wish to thank the electorate in my constituency for having placed their confidence in me once more in the past election. I shall try my best to keep their interests at heart while attending to the obligations of a minister of the Crown. I also wish to give special thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for having had the confidence and, if I may say so, Mr. Speaker, the courage-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -to entrust me with the task of Minister of Agriculture for Canada. I am still new enough to this portfolio to be able to think it is a big challenge and still new enough to thank the Prime Minister for giving me the opportunity to represent the farmers from one end of the country to the other. There may be some who may find it rather hard to accept the fact that the Minister of Agriculture does not come from western Canada. However, I must point out that I received messages from all across Canada, from farm leaders, provincial ministers of agriculture and some premiers. Only one premier, and I cannot remember which province he represents, was not complimentary.

speechtext: Who was he?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That brother of yours?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think he migrated from Nova Scotia to Saskatchewan 14 years ago.
I have lived on the farm all my life and have been an active farmer for most of my life, certainly until I was elected to the House of Commons. Those who are engaged in agriculture and who are also Members of Parliament know that being a member is a full-time job. One has no time left in which to engage in actual agricultural production if one is really doing the job demanded of a representative here. The part of Canada from which I come is the most productive of any in Canada. This is a fact of
January 16, 1973

which many people are unaware; possibly we ourselves are at fault for not yelling it loud and clear.
Many people think of Ontario as being strictly an industrialized giant. It is an agricultural giant as well; one might call it the giant of agricultural production in Canada. Farm cash receipts in 1972 in the province are likely to amount to almost $1.5 billion. Saskatchewan, this year, will be second highest in this respect. The situation is changing, if I understand it correctly; Saskatchewan is displacing Alberta, it seems, though there may be some Alberta members who will wish to disagree. However, these are the figures given to me.
Back in Roman days, Mr. Speaker, one of their old boys who had done a good deal of travelling round Europe came back to his capital and said "veni, vidi, vici". Well, I did some travelling around Canada at the end of last year. I did not conquer. I did something more. I listened and learned. Among the many things I learned was that farmers all across our land are basically the same. At the farm meetings I addressed in western Canada, when I said I was a minister of the Crown for Canadian agriculture, the Canadian Minister of Agriculture, they all responded in a more amazing fashion even than I had anticipated. They did not want me as an eastern Minister of Agriculture nor as a western Minister of Agriculture. They wanted me as a Canadian Minister of Agriculture working for the benefit of Canadian farm producers no matter in what part of the land they reside. They have more in common than the few differences which are continuously played up. They have more marketing problems in common, more production problems in common. They are competing, often, for the same domestic markets or for the same overseas markets. Differences which are brought about by circumstance or which are connected with historical habits have long since died, as far as I am concerned. All our farmers have the same desire for a stable income and they all face the same risks because of weather, disease and fluctuating markets. They are beginning to realize that some of their difficulties can best be solved by national planning, cooperation and mutual support through the assistance of their provincial governments and with the help of Ottawa.
I want to take this opportunity to thank my provincial counterparts for the courtesy they showed me on my first visit to them. I must say I found them extremely responsive and helpful, as I confirmed when I telephoned their offices to ask some of them for their opinions. It might surprise some hon. members to learn how many ministers in provincial governments answer their own telephones. I think it surprised the provincial people just as much when this minister dialed his own telephone to talk to them. I learned this from a businessman in control of a large corporation; he told me that when anyone got too big to dial his own telephone he was too big to hold the position he was occupying. As far as I am concerned, our calls in the future will be many. I intend to keep up this rapport with my provincial counterparts as long as I am Minister of Agriculture because I believe in working with them for the betterment of agriculture in Canada. Without exception they showed a good grasp of the agricultural situation in their own provinces. I feel we shall all be in a better position to improve the welfare of the farmer as a result of my having met not only the provincial ministers of agriculture but also a good number of representatives
The Address-Mr. Whelan
of farm organizations in the west, in central Canada and in the east.
I am pleased to report that the agricultural industry has experienced one of the most prosperous years on record. The trend began in 1970. It was strong in 1971, even stronger last year, and is continuing through 1973. I am also pleased to report that the farming community has made some gains in moving the industry closer to our goal of putting farm income on an equal footing with the rest of the economy over the past few years. We set a $2 billion trade export record in 1971; we set another record last year, and it looks as though we are going to set still another in 1973.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Our agricultural industry has not only met the challenges of tougher competition, international monetary problems and stiff trade restrictions but it has actually improved on its own record.
We must recognize the importance of marketing and be bold enough to say so at a time when the industry sometimes tends to be inward-looking, paying most of its attention to domestic issues. The present government has begun this task with evident success. The statistics speak for themselves. The government has helped the industry to take advantage of new and expanding agricultural product markets abroad. The result has been a dramatic improvement in prospects for the success and maintenance of our family farms. Those who have charged the present administration with being too inactive should check the record; when they do, I think they will be forced to admit they are chasing non-existent ghosts. We have set records for exports. We are continuing to increase our exports. Further, we are continuing to add new products and new customers while negotiating better trade terms for our farmers. For example, as of January 1 last year we have added 10 per cent to the number of items which could enter the United States free of tariff, bringing the total up to 30 per cent. We have negotiated an important agreement with Australia which has already opened up a money-making market for cattle semen, and we have opened the door for imports of new blood lines for our beef producers. During my discussions with cattlemen's associations and others I have found them to be as happy a group of producers as I have found in any part of our nation.
New initiatives have also been taken to send specialists abroad to help the agricultural industry open new markets. The industry is making increased use of the $10 million market development fund available to it for extending markets abroad. I think they could take even more advantage of the money provided for these groups which want to develop their own markets under our guidance and assistance by taking part in this fund. There are many examples of success but I mention only these few as an indication of what has been taking place.
I must also point out, Mr. Speaker, that ever since I have become Minister of Agriculture prices to the farmers have improved considerably. I may not have had much to do with these changes in price but, as Billy Shakespeare said,

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. Whelan
"There is a time and tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune".

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You got your boat off the beach at just about the right time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is what I encourage farmers to do this spring. I urge them to produce grain to beat the band this year, all types of grains. There is a word of caution which I put in at this point. I am purposely asking western grain producers to produce all the wheat they can produce, conscious of all this implies, and at the same time to make sure they produce even larger quantities of feed grains than they grew in previous years. Except for that reservation, my theme to producers, Mr. Speaker, is to produce grain for all they are worth and, by the way, I hope money lenders both east and west are listening. There is a clear message for them. The message is to have faith in Canada's agricultural producers and give them the backing they deserve, because I intend to do this as long as I am Minister of Agriculture.
Knowing the capacity and urge of Canadian farmers to produce, I feel it in my bones, Mr. Speaker, that farmers will grow and deliver record quantities of grain, both in the east and west. The government will sell record amounts of grain again this year. And let no one belittle the efforts made by this government to improve the meteoric rise in cash income gains made from grain sales these past two years.
Some Lady Zistras have looked into their crystal balls backward and suggested the country may lose future sales because our grain supplies have been reduced to manageable proportions. In the first place Mr. Speaker, those clairvoyants did not usefully forecast, for anyone, the drop in grain production in various countries round the world or the disastrous weather conditions in the USSR and India, or the calamities that took place in other nations last year.
Second, if anything, transportation of grain to markets has been our bottleneck and the record of improvement brought about by the assistance of this government speaks for itself. We set a shipment record in 1970, smashed that record in 1971 in spite of weather difficulties, and we are well on the way to doing even better this year. I have the utmost confidence but, as I stated before, some may say I am over-optimistic that they will do even better.
Third, these latter-day soothsayers condemn themselves out of their own mouths. They are actually suggesting that Canadian grain growers will not, indeed these soothsayers imply Canadian grain growers cannot, rise to the occasion of a market opportunity that is placed before them. That, Mr. Speaker, shows an appalling lack of knowledge of the productive capacity, the large capitalization, or the real, effective, down-to-earth, export confidence and knowhow our Canadian producers possess. But most important still, these people fail to recognize the strong urge within each farmer to produce for all he is worth, given the opportunity to do so.
I would point out here that there is hardly a nation in the world where one farm worker produces so much for his fellow man. We could make a comparison with one of the largest nations that buys so much grain from us. In

Russia, for instance, one farm worker only produces enough food for two of his fellow men. In Canada, one farm worker produces enough food for 50 of his fellow men. We take this for granted and we accept it. Many of these countries that do not have the system we have, do not have the creative ability we have and do not have the incentives we have, only wish that they could create some of these in their own nations so they would be in a better position as far as food for their own people is concerned.
Indeed, a farmer is leery of believing in the dream he may never be able to realize. Well, it is here, Mr. Speaker; his dream has come true, the opportunity to produce all the grain he can produce for good markets at acceptable prices. I know as a farmer that I do not need to tell fellow farmers all this. They sense the opportunity when it comes. But farmers like to be reassured and that is the first reason I am going on at length about this situation. I am also stressing the point in the House now because the legislators of this land should be spared the humility of underestimating the drive, initiative, optimism and resourcefulness of Canadian producers. I take my hat off to my fellow farmers for their courage, their endurance, ability and productiveness. God willing, Mr. Speaker, the harvest of 1973 in Canada will confound the critics who have little understanding of the farmer's urge to produce, even if the critics hail from rural or rural-town Canada.
The government has done a number of things to improve the quality of life in rural Canada. The Farm Credit Corporation loans policy has been changed with the proclamation of amendments to the Farm Credit Act. Young farmers under the age of 35 have benefited substantially by being able to borrow under the new conditions of Part III of the Farm Credit Act. May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned I was speaking about the Farm Credit Corporation. Under the supervised loans program, young farmers may borrow up to 75 per cent of the appraised value of land and chattels up to $100,000, and if their managerial ability is considered to be above average, loans may be drawn up to 90 per cent of their farm assets. Those are realistic loan conditions repayable over 30 years. These conditions are a witness to the faith that this government has in the ability of our new breed of young farmers today. The effort made by the Farm Credit Corporation to make loans available to younger farmers has borne fruit in the last crop year. There has been a shift, an increase, of 1J per cent in loans made to people under the age of 35 between 1970 and 1971, and 1971 and 1972. The shift is evident at the other end of the scale in that, out of a total number of loans made, there has also been a shift of 1J per cent decline in the number of loans made to people over 55 years of age.
January 16, 1973

I have some very strong views on the Farm Credit Corporation, on what it can do and what it has done as well as on what it should be doing. If any hon. members have suggestions as to what they think the Farm Credit Corporation can and should be doing to help young farmers and farmers in general, I would appreciate hearing from them. The changes will help Canadian farmers to develop more profitable family farms and I have under active consideration, as I stated, methods to improve still further the corporation's loan policy to the advantage of our producers, but I am willing to listen and accept good suggestions as to how this can be achieved.
Another program, the exhibition loans program to help agricultural societies to borrow money at very attractive interest rates over a long term payment period, is being continued. This policy has been much appreciated by those who wish to put up buildings that can be used at fall fairs and exhibitions and, equally important, which can be used for functions right through the entire year. I might add, for those who are interested in what is being done in some parts of Canada, that I met a group from western Canada this morning. They are putting up one of the best exhibitions of livestock that I have ever seen a new young organization put up. I think we should do everything we can to encourage this type of program. It helps the urban people realize what the rural people are doing in Canada.
An important new program to improve life in rural Canada is the small farms development program. The last of the programs I have signed on behalf of the federal government has been with the province of Nova Scotia. Alberta and Ontario have already implemented the program and British Columbia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and now Nova Scotia, have signed agreements.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about Manitoba?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These programs may not be what everyone would desire, but again I am open to further suggestions on how we can improve them for all of Canada. I am hopeful that the remaining four provinces will join in the near future. If they do not, we have the authority to provide these benefits for those farmers under a federal program if their province does not wish to participate in the program. The discussions with the province of Quebec on this subject, which bogged down a little, have, I am pleased to say, been put back on the track with every indication that we will come to a mutual understanding. I might say that one of the best discussions I had on my trip across Canada was with my counterpart in the province of Quebec, Mr. Tuppin. He understood the problems, he presented his viewpoint in a factual way, and I am sure that we were not far apart in our positions on many issues that have confronted farmers in the province of Quebec.
The Canadian agriculture industry continues to become more specialized every year and, because of that, this government continues to support the industry and farmers through research programs in the Department of Agriculture which has the reputation for doing some of the finest research work in the agricultural world. I do not think that even our own citizens are aware of this. They are even some events taking place of which many mem-
The Address-Mr. Whelan
bers of the House are not aware, and every day I am learning something new that is going on in agricultural research, either in livestock, grains or horticulture. Many of us are not aware of what is going on because not enough is being said, and what is being said is not being said loudly and clearly enough.
As a result of our support, Canadians farmers have achieved a remarkable record of performance. They not only produce some of the best farm products in the world, but they do it more efficiently. All of us in the House, and hon. members from rural communities in particular, realize that it is not always smooth sailing and that in farming there are many problems which fall beyond the scope of any individual farmer, problems which can more properly be handled by government. It is for this reason that the government made hog deficiency payments of up to $1,000 per producer to offset the pork market glut of 18 months ago, caused mainly by heavy production in the United States.
Support for the dairy industry has been continued and was increased during this dairy year, taking into account the increasing cost of production and the improved market conditions. The leadership of the federal government, in stabilizing the dairy industry, has been very successful and this program has paid off both for Canada and for dairy farmers. It has held production and incomes at reasonable levels. Without this support, our industrial milk producing industry would have been bankrupt long ago, thus creating a severe loss not only for our dairy farmers but for all Canadian consumers. There are some who complain about the 17 days supply of butter that we will have to import this winter to supply the Canadian consumer, but I would remind those people that it is better to be in that position than to have a small surplus bearing down heavily on the price of all the dairy products and consequently on the total income of all producers across the country.
In my opinion, the National Dairy Commission is one of the most efficiently operated marketing organizations in Canada, and one of the things that I specifically like about it is its control over imports. I like the way it operates and the way in which it brings imports into Canada when they are needed and puts them on the market at a price that the consumers can afford to pay. At the same time, the actions of the Commission do not depress the price to the producers but provide stability to the industry. When one checks the price range of the dairy products in the last four years, one realizes that if all other parts of the agriculture industry were run in this fashion, inflation would not be as rampant as it is today.
The federal government intends to continue its support of the dairy industry. More than 90 per cent of our industrial milk production now comes from provinces which have entered the market sharing quota program because of the agreements with the prairie provinces this past year. I would also note, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Dairy Commission has been quick on the draw to take advantage of the situation of skim milk powder shortage in the United States. This quick action has allowed Canada to supply part of the American requirement at

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. Whelan
favourable prices to our milk producers. This was done by tender.
The disaster aid program, put together jointly with Quebec and Ontario, has added up to one of the biggest aid programs ever for farmers experiencing losses due to wet weather. The farmers of the Peace River area of Alberta and of British Columbia have been offered a similar program of help through the co-operation of their provincial governments. The programs of assistance are not entirely alike because in western Canada there are already such programs as the PFAA, the Grassland Incentive Program, and advance payments on unharvested grain, programs tailored for different circumstances.
Crop losses and disasters due to weather are not new to agriculture. They are a part of the natural risk of farming, and I think most farmers accept that fact. But just the same they are disasters, and every government in every nation tries to plan to offset the difficulties that these create. In Canada the federal and provincial governments have worked for many years to develop a crop insurance program to overcome these problems, and to offer some level of security to farmers. We have had several years of experience with the crop insurance program, and we have had recent experience with the disasters in the Peace River area, eastern Ontario and western Quebec.

These problems concerning crop insurance are hard to overcome. In view of these difficulties I believe it is time to re-examine the entire crop insurance program, to set out goals firmly in mind, and to develop a better program. During my trip across Canada, there was not one provincial minister of agriculture who did not bring this to my attention. They want the real principle of insurance embodied in crop insurance. They feel it is not in the program at the present time.
Again, I am open to suggestions from anyone who has any ideas on how we can improve the crop insurance program. I have already received some ideas from hon. members, and I intend to use them when bringing forward new legislation. As indicated in the throne speech, Mr. Speaker, the House will be asked "to amend the crop insurance act to allow the government to reimburse provinces to a maximum of 50 per cent of premiums paid under contracts of insurance, thereby reducing costs of insurance to individual farmers." As I have stated, I, and I believe the farmers are willing to go further. I am hopeful that an acceptable proposal can be worked out with the provincial departments of agriculture and with farmers so that we can come up with a crop insurance scheme which will be popularly acceptable to the farming community and will be along true insurance lines.

Because we have kept our ear to the ground and acted to help producers across the country, the government implemented the fowl slaughter program which quickly brought egg production back in line with demand, and allowed the establishment of the first national farm products marketing agency. We have also brought about changes in the rates of feed freight assistance to offset changes in cost, introduced a potato support program which helped the Maritime growers to overcome a difficult period of surplus production, and continued the federal government support for the sugar beet industry.
In the grain and oil seeds marketing system the number of changes introduced since 1968 have culminated in the success of our marketing effort, and have proven the wisdom of the changes made in the regulations. But we do not plan to sit still in the coming year. Although we already have a new set of wheat grades, a new quota delivery system, a grassland incentive program, improved transportation records at the Lakehead and Vancouver, and many other improvements, still further improvements are being considered for the coming year.
Hon. members who may not be familiar with the subject should check their old agriculture committee reports and see what we recommended six years ago to improve grain handling facilities both on the coast and in the St. Lawrence Seaway. If they do, they will realize that hon. members at that time had futuristic ideas and attitudes.
When talking about the export records that have been set, I do not wish to leave the impression that it was the government that set these records on its own. It took a great deal of co-operation between government and the entire grain producing, transporting, insuring, shipping and exporting industries. It required gumption to find the weak spots, identify them, acknowledge them, and then move to make the changes that brought about the desired improvements. I hope this co-operation will continue. Indeed, recognition of the validity of this approach has been indicated by the establishment of a new branch within the Department of Agriculture to try the same formula with other commodities, commodity groups, and sections of the agriculture industry.
One of the major tasks of the new food systems branch concerns the feed grain industry. Right now we are talking with the industry about the new feed grains policy for Canada, taking into account the many changes made in production, transportation, international markets, and our own domestic livestock industry needs. Again, as indicated in the Speech from the Throne, the government supports the principle of an equitable relationship of prices of feed grain to livestock feeders in various areas of Canada. It is the intention of the government to implement, before the next crop year, procedures that will insure the optimum development of the feed grain and livestock industries within Canada.
There are many things I could say about the agriculture industry, Mr. Speaker, but I realize that if I said all that I have written here, I would take up more than my fair share of the time of the House. However, I do wish to take a few more minutes to complete a few points.
One of the biggest changes in agricultural policy introduced by the government has been the passage of the National Farm Products Marketing Act. I am convinced
January 16, 1973

that national marketing agencies hold the key to major improvements within the agriculture industry, and will enable farmers to increase their income considerably. It is too early to judge the success of this legislation, but I am convinced that in years ahead we will look back and approve the persistence and foresight shown in having this idea put into the law of the land.
I want to take this opportunity to express my appreciation to the group of leaders who have been chosen to head the National Farm Products Marketing Council. Their leadership and tact have already done much to convince the doubters and sceptics that national marketing agencies can be a good thing and should be given a chance. The first national marketing agency, the one for eggs, is just now getting into operation. As this new group of men take up the challenge I am sure many farmers will find that national marketing agencies have a great deal to offer them, and that the trade as well as consumers will find these organizations to be to their advantage. I expect that we will have other national marketing agencies in operation before the end of the year. I have received notice from turkey and broiler producers that they wish to have a marketing plan, and before long they will want a national inquiry into the merits of such a plan.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the agriculture industry is certainly in a much stronger position today than it was four years ago. The leadership, policies and programs initiated by my predecessors in this portfolio have had a great deal to do with the turn around, the better fortunes, and the good outlook for the industry and its producers. Problems and challenges remain to be tackled. I do not intend to rest on the achievements of my predecessors but will take up the challenge from here. There are great potentials for Canadian agriculture, and I am confident that we have the policies and programs which will help Canadian farmers to reach their full potential.
Because farming and the food industry form only part of the fabric of Canadian life, the Minister of Agriculture does not have a czar's influence even in his own area of jurisdiction. But I can assure hon. members that this minister will defend farmers' interests in this country with all the political skill that farmers are reputed to be able to muster, and as a member of the cabinet I will see to it that this is done within a framework of general conditions favourable to Canadian consumers.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time that I have had the honour of addressing the House of Commons, an honour that I am sure all Canadians would prize. Like many other members who have spoken in this debate, I should like to begin by joining in an accolade to you and your associates for the way in which you are presiding over the affairs of this House.
We are here to debate the Speech from the Throne and I should like to begin by complimenting its authors, both seen and unseen, for they have produced a remarkable document. However, I am sure they would agree if I were to suggest to hon. members opposite, that with a little
The Address-Mr. Stackhouse
imagination we could think of ways in which it might have been improved. This afternoon I should like to suggest a few proposals which might have been included.
For example, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne might have said something such as this: "The government will try to reduce unemployment in Canada by giving a job to every defeated Liberal candidate." Or, it might have said something such as this: "As a contribution to Canadian culture, the government will commission a national film board documentary on the election. It will be called "How the West was Lost". Or, "The government will authorize a CBC television serial: one part to be about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1968. It will be called; "How to Succeed in Politics Without Really Trying." The second part will be on the Prime Minister in 1972 and it will be called: "How to Try in Politics Without Really Succeeding".

Or, "The government will attempt a bold innovation in politics: Liberal ministers and Conservative policies."
Instead of "fuddleduddle" we now have "flip-flop". In the throne speech the government "flipped", because in the election the government "flopped".

speechtext:
None the less, the throne speech is a remarkable document. It expresses the politics of "something for everybody"-or almost everybody.
It is not clear what the government intends for the kind of citizen about whom I want to speak mainly-the middle Canadians. I have the privilege of representing Scarborough East. With 87,000 electors it is one of the largest ridings in Canada and represents a "mix" of the great diversity one finds in the Canada of today. Scarborough East is totally within metropolitan Toronto, but it still has farms as well as high rise apartments and residential neighbourhoods. Most of its people are of British ancestry or origin, but it also has large numbers from every part of Europe, from Asia, from Africa, from the Middle East, from Latin America, from the Caribbean. Many of its people are young and over 25 per cent are in school, college or university. However, the riding includes a growing number of senior citizens.
With all this diversity, however, there is something that the people have in common. Most are what can be called "middle Canadians"; they are not affluent, not impoverished, but are earning enough to be self-supporting; they are not "fat-cats," not "bums," but are working people.
The Prime Minister has professed to be concerned, and rightly so, about alienation-alienation of the west-even as he has been about alienation of Quebec. I should like to put it to the House that we need to be equally concerned about another kind of alienation. There is in Canada today not only regional alienation but sociological alienation. For many middle Canadians there is a growing unease about the direction our society has been following and the direction this government has been leading.
I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of alienation which many people are experiencing is partly

January 16, 1973
The Address-Mr. Stackhouse due to the way in which the government seems to have become removed from the people. Government in Canada has become of such behemoth proportions, and seems so complex in its proceedings, that the average person can say of the government it is his government in name only. One way in which the government of Canada might come closer to the people is by taking steps to open membership in this House of Commons to more and more Canadians.
One of the difficulties that people find when standing for election to the House of Commons is that they usually have to give up their jobs. This imposes upon their families a financial burden that most men and women do not feel justified in asking. I would suggest that we need to reform our election practices so that membership of this parliament can be sought by people of all occupations. If parliament is to be truly representative it must be the nation in small. It must be representative of all religions, races, ethnic origins, languages and so on, but it also must be representative of occupations. Parliament has been dominated too long by too few occupations. I suggest that we should consider a proposal that parliament enact legislation requiring all employers to permit employees with two years seniority to become candidates without fear of losing their jobs. Employers would be required to give such employees leave of absence during the election campaign, such leave to be without pay. Employers should be pledged to grant leave of absence without pay to any employee elected to the House of Commons. Should an employee seek re-election after one term he or she would be deemed to have resigned since it could be interpreted that he or she had begun a new career.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of obligation is comparable to what was required of employers during wartime when they were expected to keep jobs open for employees who served with the armed forces. If we can require employers to make this kind of commitment during the war to those who would serve their country, surely we can do it in peace. Parliament should not be primarily a place of privilege but a vocation of service open to many.
The alienation of middle Canadians is accented by the way social forces make the local community and single individual seem insignificant. Much is said in this House about participation, involvement, consultation, but often more is said than is done. It is frequently the tendency of government to announce first and consult later-maybe. For example, last week the construction of three limited dividend apartment projects in Scarborough was announced. They are to be funded by the federal government. Community associations are concerned about this, not because they reject their social responsibility to low income citizens but because they are concerned about the impact of high rise building on family neighbourhoods and about the ingress of large numbers of children in such areas with already limited recreational and service facilities. When one Ontario Housing corporation project was proposed early last spring, a protest meeting assembled 1,000 ratepayers to voice these concerns, and the federal government take them seriously. The Ontario government listened to these people and the project was stopped. The government of that province has also initiated a study of the future of public housing in Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I propose that the federal government should initiate a study of public housing in Scarborough. This study should involve all three levels of government and aim at developing more effective ways of meeting these housing needs than having the people together in buildings that often soon come to be looked upon as ghettos. Scarborough has about 15 per cent of the population of metro Toronto but about 33 per cent of the Ontario housing located in metro plus the limited dividend apartments. These housing projects, being partially or wholly financed from federal funds, show the great federal involvement in public housing in this municipality. I put it to the House that before any more projects are undertaken in Scarborough the federal government should invite the province and municipality to co-operate in a study that would indicate the best direction to follow in future. Part of the value of this study would be the demonstration to the community that it has a voice which is heard and is taken seriously.
Another reason many middle income Canadians feel alienated from society results from the development of a permissive approach to life. There is a permissiveness abroad that they often seem to believe is encouraged by the government. What the middle income Canadian wants is the rule of law to be respected. Civilization demands this because a civilization is a society that has learned to live together under the rule of law. Western society has come to take that rule for granted, but one of the results of urbanization has been the decline of that rule. In the United States the streets of the city are emptied at night by fear. Fear turns a key in every door and people lock themselves in their homes as though they were prisoners in cells. That can happen in Canada, too. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that we need a "firming up" in our administration of law.

The graduated income tax was based on the concept of distributive justice-the belief that the strong should bear more of the burden than the weak. However, in an inflationary economy the graduated income tax has become a way by which middle Canadians are being penalized for trying to keep abreast of inflation. When they are successful in raising their dollar income to meet the decline in the dollar's purchasing power, they find themselves taxed at a higher rate. This often means not only that they must pay more tax dollars but, also, that a higher percentage of their income must go to the government. They thus find themselves robbed of much they had gained. What they thought was progress turns out to be a penalty.
